chunks: From him, from Ali ibn Abi Hamzah, from Abu Basir, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

The Mudabbir (a slave manumitted upon his master's death) is a slave, and his master has the right to revoke the manumission; if he wishes, he may sell him, if he wishes, he may gift him, and if he wishes, he may marry him off.
And if his master leaves him in the state of Mudabbir and no incident occurs in him until the master dies, the Mudabbir becomes free when the master dies.
He is in the position of a man who made a will, then changed his mind later and altered it before his death; if he left it and did not alter it until he died, it is executed.

key_terms.أَمَّهَرَهُ: He married him off (gave him a wife).
key_terms.الْمُدَبَّرُ: Mudabbir: A slave manumitted upon the master's death, pending the master's revocation.
key_terms.تَدْبِيرٌ: Manumission deferred until death; the act of declaring a slave free upon death.

ai.seo_question: What is the legal ruling for a Mudabbir slave if the master dies without revoking the manumission?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Isfahani clarifies the legal mechanism of *tadbir*, where a master’s declaration of freedom is contingent upon his survival; it establishes that the master retains full discretion to revoke this status by selling, gifting, or marrying the slave before death. The analogy to a revocable will (*wasiyya*) highlights the Shia juristic view that *tadbir* is not an immediate transfer of freedom but a conditional promise that solidifies only upon the master's death without intervening changes. This ruling underscores the balance between the master's property rights and the slave's potential for emancipation within the framework of *fiqh al-jafari*.
